items.title: 6.3.5 Similarly, we find condition of Tangency for other parabolas

source_refs.note: Book p. 187-188: 6.3.5 (heading repeats the 6.3.4 sentence); unlabelled worked problem: tangent yy1 = 2a(x + x1) and normal to y^2 = 4ax at (x1, y1).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The printed heading of 6.3.5 repeats the last sentence of 6.3.4 ("Similarly, we can find condition of tangency for other parabolas"). What the book actually prints under it is a worked problem, without an example number: the tangent and the normal to \(y^{2} = 4ax\) at a given point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\). We present it below under its own heading, and after it we add (as our own material) the tangency conditions for the other three standard parabolas, which is what the heading announces.
Worked problem: tangent and normal at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\)

blocks.title: Worked problem
blocks.problem: Find the equations of the tangent and normal to the parabola \(y^{2} = 4ax\) at the point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\).
steps:
Given: the parabola \(y^{2} = 4ax\) and a point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) on it, so \(y_{1}^{2} = 4ax_{1}\).
To find: the tangent and the normal at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\).
Method: slope of the tangent from \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), point-slope form; then use \(y_{1}^{2} = 4ax_{1}\) to simplify. The normal has the negative reciprocal slope.

Step 1: Slope of the tangent
Differentiating \(y^{2} = 4ax\) with respect to \(x\), we obtain
\[2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4a\]
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2a}{y}\]
Thus, the slope of the tangent at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) is
\[\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_{1}, y_{1})} = \dfrac{2a}{y_{1}}\]
Why: implicit differentiation; \(\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = 2y\frac{dy}{dx}\) by the chain rule. (We need \(y_{1} \ne 0\); at the vertex the tangent is the vertical line \(x = 0\).)

Step 2: Point-slope form
\[y - y_{1} = \dfrac{2a}{y_{1}}(x - x_{1})\]
Multiplying both sides by \(y_{1}\), we get
\[yy_{1} - y_{1}^{2} = 2ax - 2ax_{1}\]
Rearranging terms,
\[yy_{1} - 2ax = y_{1}^{2} - 2ax_{1}\]
Why: a line through \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) with slope \(m\) is \(y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})\); multiplying by \(y_{1}\) removes the fraction.

Step 3: Use that the point is on the parabola
Since \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) lies on the parabola, \(y_{1}^{2} = 4ax_{1}\). Substituting this value,
\[yy_{1} - 2ax = 4ax_{1} - 2ax_{1} = 2ax_{1}\]
Bringing all terms to one side,
\[yy_{1} - 2ax - 2ax_{1} = 0\]
which simplifies to
\[yy_{1} = 2a(x + x_{1})\]
This is the required equation of the tangent.
Why: replacing \(y_{1}^{2}\) by \(4ax_{1}\) leaves only first powers of \(x_{1}, y_{1}\), giving the short, easy-to-remember form.

Step 4: The normal
The slope of the normal is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent. Hence,
\[\text{Slope of the normal} = -\dfrac{y_{1}}{2a}\]
Using the point-slope form, the equation of the normal is
\[y - y_{1} = -\dfrac{y_{1}}{2a}(x - x_{1})\]
Why: normal \(\perp\) tangent, so \(m_{1}m_{2} = -1\): \(\frac{2a}{y_{1}} \times \left(-\frac{y_{1}}{2a}\right) = -1\).

Check:
Take \(a = 1\) and the point \((1, 2)\) on \(y^{2} = 4x\). Tangent: \(2y = 2(x + 1)\), i.e. \(y = x + 1\). Substituting in \(y^{2} = 4x\): \((x + 1)^{2} = 4x\), i.e. \((x - 1)^{2} = 0\), a repeated root, so the line touches at \((1, 2)\). It also agrees with 6.3.4: slope \(m = 1\), \(c = \frac{a}{m} = 1\). Normal: \(y - 2 = -(x - 1)\), i.e. \(x + y - 3 = 0\), slope \(-1\), perpendicular to slope 1.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick rule to remember the tangent (our addition): in the equation of the curve replace \(y^{2}\) by \(yy_{1}\) and \(x\) by \(\frac{x + x_{1}}{2}\):
\[y^{2} = 4ax \ \to\ yy_{1} = 4a\cdot\dfrac{x + x_{1}}{2}\]
This is the same rule as for the circle in 6.2.2, whose Note says it works for all conics. The normal can also be written without fractions:
\[y_{1}x + 2ay - x_{1}y_{1} - 2ay_{1} = 0\]

Substituting \(y = mx + c\) in each standard equation and setting the discriminant equal to zero (exactly as in 6.3.4) gives the condition of tangency; the tangent at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) follows from the rule above.

header: \(y = mx + c\) is a tangent if
blocks.caption: Our summary: tangency conditions and tangents for the four standard parabolas

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example: the condition for \(x^{2} = 4ay\). Put \(y = mx + c\):
\[x^{2} = 4a(mx + c)\]
\[x^{2} - 4amx - 4ac = 0\]
Equal roots: \(D = 16a^{2}m^{2} + 16ac = 0\), so \(c = -am^{2}\). For example, \(x^{2} = 4y\) (\(a = 1\)) is touched by \(y = 2x - 4\): \(x^{2} - 8x + 16 = (x - 4)^{2} = 0\), at \((4, 4)\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: For a parabola that is not in standard form (as in Exercise 6.3, Q9) do not use these formulas; differentiate the given equation, find the slope at the point, and use the point-slope form. For a point given by its parameter (Q8), put \(x_{1} = at^{2}\), \(y_{1} = 2at\) into \(yy_{1} = 2a(x + x_{1})\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Leaving \(y_{1}^{2}\) in the tangent instead of replacing it by \(4ax_{1}\); the answer is then correct but not simplified.
2. Using \(\frac{2a}{y_{1}}\) as the slope of the normal; that is the tangent's slope. The normal's slope is \(-\frac{y_{1}}{2a}\).
3. Writing the tangent as \(yy_{1} = 4a(x + x_{1})\): the factor is \(2a\), because \(x\) is replaced by the average \(\frac{x + x_{1}}{2}\).
4. Applying the formulas at a point that is not on the parabola. First check \(y_{1}^{2} = 4ax_{1}\).
